articles.title: Build for the future climate — or waste trillions of dollars
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 23 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03722-8Development planning needs a permanent system that connects climate projections to the decisions that shape what infrastructure gets built.
articles.content:
“Prepare for El Niño”, the World Meteorological Organization warned earlier this year. Governments are responding by adjusting agricultural practices and securing water supplies. But climate measures should not begin when a hazardous event approaches, they should be part of a wider strategy of planning for a warmer future.

Repeated disasters cause immense disruption to people’s lives and livelihoods, and the economic loss and damage can add up to trillions of dollars. Climate warnings and actions taken in anticipation of disasters can help to reduce the impact on people and economies. But their effectiveness is constrained by existing limitations, such as a community’s access to resources and infrastructure.

Such vulnerabilities must be addressed at their source, when decisions about development and infrastructure are being made, so that climate risks are reduced through better planning rather than through reactive responses to individual events. Decisions about the location and capacity of reservoirs, agricultural drainage systems and the design of cities and transport infrastructure, for instance, cannot be changed easily once they have been made.

Much of what is being built now will shape societies for decades. To meet global climate and development objectives by 2030, nearly US$7 trillion of infrastructure investment is needed annually1. Global annual infrastructure spending is projected to increase from $4.4 trillion in 2024 to $6.9 trillion by 20502. But it will be wasted if projects are designed inadequately for the climate conditions that people will face.

The super El Niño is more than a climate shock — it’s a health one, too

Decisions for development projects are being hampered because climate projections are often not integrated into planning processes. Another challenge is the limited availability of reliable, decision-relevant climate information for the 5–30-year period — an intermediate timescale between seasonal forecasts and long-term climate projections that is particularly relevant for planning major infrastructure such as roads and reservoirs3.

Climate services can provide this information. Scientists can improve climate projections. Development planners can assess projects. But unless these functions are connected within the development process, the system as a whole remains reactive.

A common operating system would change that. Government ministries that oversee development would determine which planning decisions need to consider climate information. Planning institutions would ensure that climate assessments are undertaken and considered as part of investment approval for climate-sensitive projects. Climate agencies would provide the scientific information, which would improve both planning and science. Here, I outline how such a system would work.

Set up climate-planning units

A central government planning institution should establish a small climate-planning unit within it, not separately. Corresponding units could be set up in state or subnational planning institutions when appropriate. In countries without central planning institutions, the same functions could be assigned to existing government institutions.

The central unit would set common standards, consolidate information needs across sectors and jurisdictions, coordinate with national climate agencies and ensure that climate considerations are incorporated into the planning and appraisal of projects of national significance. Subnational units would apply the framework to local projects and feed emerging requirements back to the central unit.

Responsibilities should be made explicit. Ministries should identify the climate information needed to support various sectors. Planning institutions would coordinate those needs and ensure that such climate information informs investment decisions. Climate agencies would produce the underlying scientific information and ensure its technical accuracy and quality.

This division matters. The proposal is not to make development planners become climate scientists, nor to make climate agencies become development authorities. It is to give them a permanent institutional connection.

Require climate foresight

The rules governing public investment in development should be changed to follow this principle: funding for a major climate-sensitive project should not be approved without a demonstration that it has been designed for the climate it is expected to face.

Governments should request climate assessments for large, long-lived and climate-sensitive projects before approving funds. Assessments should be provided early enough in the process to influence the location, technology, scale and design of a project. For a new reservoir, for example, the relevant planning unit would identify the climate conditions that the reservoir is likely to face during its operational lifetime, with implications for where and how it is built.

A climate-planning unit would not decide whether the project should proceed; it would certify that the relevant climate risks have been assessed and that reasonable alternatives have been considered. Its assessment would be considered as part of an investment appraisal alongside economic, technical, social and environmental factors.

Let plans shape climate analyses

To be effective, the system must connect three functions: development demand, climate analysis and investment approval.

Ministries should periodically identify the climate information needed for their forthcoming development decisions. The central planning unit should consolidate these requests and work with climate agencies to determine what information can be provided, what projects require fresh analysis and when investment for climate observations, modelling or scientific capacity is needed.

Kenya’s government is implementing measures to reduce flooding from rivers.Credit: James Wakibia/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty

This comprehensive approach would provide climate scientists with clear directives from the development system. It would encourage them to improve climate projections for specific regions, over a 5–30-year typical planning horizon, and for distinct sectors. It would also reduce the need for individual development projects to commission their own climate analyses, which can be patchy and inconsistent.

An analysis of six generations of assessment reports from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change found, for instance, that inconsistent climate projections across many low- and middle-income countries were complicating adaptation and long-term planning efforts4. For example, in some regions, precipitation was projected by one assessment to increase, and by the next to decrease, with successive views bouncing back and forth.

Such disagreements undermine a region’s ability to make long-term investments. They increase the likelihood of costly misallocation of funds, maladaptation to climate risks and infrastructure being developed that is ill-suited to future climate conditions. Dams, cities and transport corridors cannot be easily redesigned or rebuilt once constructed.

This challenge is compounded by the fact that climate models perform poorly across many climate-vulnerable regions. In South Asia, for example, simulations of temperature and precipitation can differ from observed values by as much as 25% and 100%, respectively5. Such biases limit the reliability of model-based climate information for guiding long-term development decisions.

That’s why the proposed climate-informed planning units would ensure that climate agencies’ work is guided by clearly articulated development needs and that the information they provide is reliable and fit for development planning. Importantly, they would not be a replacement for other climate services, which can remain focused on providing accurate information for a wide range of sectors6,7. The aim is to bridge a specific gap between climate information and development.

Make the system learn

A climate assessment for a development project should not become obsolete as soon as the work is approved. Both central and subnational planning units should regularly monitor whether new climate observations or scientific assessments change the climate risks identified. If they do, an updated assessment should be returned to the planning authority.

Global emissions slow — but world hurtles towards 2 °C of warming

The units should evaluate whether the climate information generated by the system is useful. Regular technical reviews would compare climate projections with observations and assess whether the information remains fit for planning purposes. Institutional reviews conducted by climate-planning units could also examine whether big projects have incorporated climate foresight and whether it influenced their designs.

These reviews would create a feedback loop. Development decisions would determine what information is needed, which could be satisfied by climate-science and investment-appraisal processes. Data from implemented projects would then be fed back into the system to update climate information and plans going forwards.

Implement the system

It highlights a systemic approach that could benefit societies globally by ensuring infrastructure investments are climate-resilient, thus preventing waste of trillions of dollars and protecting communities. The focus on institutionalizing climate foresight in planning processes represents a significant positive real-world impact with broad societal and environmental benefits.
articles.personality_title: New system aims to make infrastructure ready for future climates
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Climate change is causing more extreme weather events like floods and droughts. These disasters disrupt lives and cost trillions of dollars. Governments often react to these events instead of planning ahead for a warmer future.

**What happened** – Experts propose creating permanent climate-planning units within governments to connect climate science with development decisions. These units would ensure that new infrastructure projects, like reservoirs and roads, are designed to handle the climate conditions expected over their lifetime. Planning would require climate assessments before approving funding for major projects.

**Impact** – This approach would help avoid building infrastructure that can fail or become useless because it wasn’t designed for future weather patterns. It would save money and protect communities by reducing risks from climate disasters. The system also encourages better cooperation between scientists and planners, improving the quality and usefulness of climate information.

**What's next step** – Governments would set up these climate-planning units and change rules so that climate assessments become a required part of project approval. The system would regularly update climate data and project designs to keep pace with new information. This ongoing process helps keep infrastructure safe and effective as climate conditions change.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Creating permanent climate-planning units will help governments build infrastructure that can withstand future climate challenges and avoid costly mistakes.

articles.title: The world doesn’t need solar or wind — it needs solar and wind
articles.content:
Humans are still hunter gatherers — not for food, but for energy: Much like we once roamed the landscape digging up edible roots, today we gouge the planet for coal, oil, and gas. But just as we eventually adopted agriculture, we’re starting to farm the wind and sun. Because we can’t stop our star from setting, though, we must combine solar panels with large batteries, which load up on energy during the day and distribute it at night.

According to a new report from the energy think tank Ember, diversifying the electrical grid by adding wind power is a massive opportunity to reduce costs. “If you rely on one crop and that crop is having a bad year, you’re going to be struggling,” said Daan Walter, principal at Ember and author of the new report. “The same is true for wind and solar, and it’s the reason why diversification is so important. We’re now building batteries, and those are effectively the silos where we store the sunshine for later in the day.”

The report found that in the United States and Europe, you’d need 20 hours of battery storage to achieve 90 percent uptime for solar. Add wind power to the system and that drops to just 12 hours, meaning you don’t have to install as many costly lithium-ion batteries. Accordingly, worldwide this technique could drop the median cost of meeting that 90 percent demand from $105 per megawatt-hour with solar to $86 with additional wind power. (You can see the potential of that wind power in the map below — it alone can more than meet electricity demand.)

Ember

One of the challenges with solar power is the planet’s pesky seasons. If you’re at the equator, you bask in sunlight all year round, bathing your panels in constant rays. In that case, you don’t really need wind power, if you have a lot of panels plugged into batteries.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Move farther north or south, though, and you’re getting much less solar power as the winter drags on. To ensure that everyone’s getting enough juice during those dark days, you’d need lots of batteries and what are called “long-duration energy storage” techniques. These include pumped storage hydropower, in which you use wind or solar power to pump water uphill into a reservoir, then release it to spin turbines when you need electricity, giving you a bigger (and longer-lasting) surplus of energy than with lithium-ion batteries.

Ember

Now imagine northern grids that hum with plenty of solar power in the long days of summer, but can also exploit the wind in the long nights of winter. In the map above, you’ll see the savings from combining the two are greatest in the northern parts of the planet. The report found that without wind, solar and batteries can achieve 90 percent uptime near the equator for less than $60 per megawatt-hour, in contrast to areas above 55 degrees north costing $280. Add wind to the mix and at every latitude, the costs dip below $100.

“At least from a cost perspective and a reliability perspective, you can have clean power at competitive enough prices,” said Al-Amin Bugaje, a research fellow studying the electrical sector at the climate solutions nonprofit Project Drawdown, who wasn’t involved in the research. That means not having to keep developing fossil-fuel power infrastructure.

Combining solar and wind could also help ward off the dreaded dunkelflaute — literally, “dark doldrums,” from the German — also known as anticyclonic gloom. These are extended periods where there’s simultaneously too little sun and too little wind, which is obviously a problem for panels and turbines. The Ember analysis finds that on average across the world, this lull for solar happens about four times a year, and for wind around eight. “That’s very annoying, because then you need to store lots of energy beforehand,” Walter said. “You need to build an awful lot of batteries to actually get that done.”

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Ember

That, of course, raises costs. But, Walter found, by combining wind and solar, you instead experience a dunkelflaute on average every four years. (You can see this visualized in the graph above — green and blue are solar and wind droughts, respectively, and dark blue is both happening simultaneously.) Ideally, there’d be enough battery and long-duration storage on the grid to get utilities through those stretches without having to spin up gas or coal power plants.

If you can’t relate to the farming metaphor of diversifying energy like diversifying crops, consider your retirement portfolio: Instead of buying one stock that can crash, investing in lots of companies spreads the risk. Ideally, in a few decades you’re looking at a steadily rising curve on a graph. “You want to put everything in an ETF or in an index with a basket of really good options or companies,” said Bugaje. “Over a long period of time, you’re safe that you’re going in the top right corner direction.”
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a significant and practical advancement in renewable energy strategy by combining solar and wind power with battery storage to reduce costs and increase reliability globally. This has broad environmental and societal benefits by enabling cleaner, more affordable energy and reducing dependence on fossil fuels. The detailed explanation of energy diversification, cost savings, and mitigation of energy shortfalls provides substantial context and substance.
articles.personality_title: Combining solar and wind power cuts costs and boosts clean energy reliability
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – People have long depended on natural resources for energy, like coal and oil. Now, to fight climate change and reduce pollution, many countries are turning to renewable energy sources like solar and wind power. But both solar and wind have challenges because the sun doesn’t always shine and the wind doesn’t always blow.

**What happened** – A new report from the energy research group Ember shows that using both solar panels and wind turbines together, along with big batteries to store energy, can make electricity cheaper and more reliable. The study found that in places like the United States and Europe, adding wind power means you need fewer expensive batteries to keep the lights on 90% of the time.

**Impact** – This combination lowers the cost of electricity from $105 to $86 per megawatt-hour on average, making clean energy more affordable. It also helps solve a problem called "dunkelflaute," times when there’s little sun and little wind at the same time. By using both energy sources, these problem times happen much less often, so power grids can rely less on fossil fuels like coal and gas.

**What's next step** – Energy planners can use these findings to design better power systems that mix solar, wind, and storage. This approach can be especially helpful in northern regions where winter days are short and solar power alone isn’t enough. Over time, this could lead to cleaner, cheaper electricity worldwide and less need to build new fossil fuel power plants.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Combining solar and wind power with battery storage makes clean energy more affordable and reliable, reducing the need for fossil fuels everywhere on Earth.
articles.personality_title_fr: Associer solaire et éolien réduit les coûts et améliore la fiabilité de l’énergie propre
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Depuis longtemps, les humains utilisent des ressources naturelles comme le charbon et le pétrole pour produire de l’énergie. Aujourd’hui, pour lutter contre le changement climatique, beaucoup de pays se tournent vers des énergies renouvelables comme le solaire et l’éolien. Mais le soleil ne brille pas toujours et le vent ne souffle pas tout le temps.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Un nouveau rapport du groupe de recherche énergétique Ember montre qu’en combinant panneaux solaires, éoliennes et grandes batteries de stockage, on peut rendre l’électricité moins chère et plus fiable. L’étude révèle qu’aux États-Unis et en Europe, ajouter de l’éolien permet de réduire le nombre de batteries coûteuses nécessaires pour assurer l’électricité 90 % du temps.

**Impact** – Cette combinaison fait baisser le coût de l’électricité de 105 à 86 dollars par mégawattheure en moyenne, rendant l’énergie propre plus accessible. Elle aide aussi à résoudre un problème appelé « dunkelflaute », des périodes où il y a peu de soleil et peu de vent en même temps. En utilisant les deux sources, ces périodes se produisent beaucoup moins souvent, ce qui réduit la dépendance aux énergies fossiles comme le charbon et le gaz.

**Prochaine étape** – Les planificateurs énergétiques peuvent utiliser ces résultats pour concevoir de meilleurs systèmes qui mélangent solaire, éolien et stockage. Cette méthode est particulièrement utile dans les régions nordiques où les journées d’hiver sont courtes et où le solaire seul ne suffit pas. À long terme, cela pourrait conduire à une électricité plus propre, moins chère et accessible dans le monde entier, avec moins de centrales fossiles.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – Associer solaire, éolien et batteries rend l’énergie propre plus abordable et fiable, réduisant partout le besoin d’énergies fossiles.
articles.personality_title_es: Combinar energía solar y eólica reduce costos y mejora la confiabilidad de la energía limpia
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Durante mucho tiempo, las personas han usado recursos naturales como el carbón y el petróleo para obtener energía. Hoy, para combatir el cambio climático, muchos países están usando energías renovables como la solar y la eólica. Pero el sol no siempre brilla y el viento no siempre sopla.

**Qué pasó** – Un nuevo informe del grupo de investigación energética Ember muestra que usar paneles solares y turbinas eólicas juntos, junto con grandes baterías para almacenar energía, puede hacer que la electricidad sea más barata y confiable. El estudio encontró que en países como Estados Unidos y Europa, agregar energía eólica reduce la cantidad de baterías costosas necesarias para mantener la electricidad funcionando el 90% del tiempo.

**Impacto** – Esta combinación reduce el costo de la electricidad de 105 a 86 dólares por megavatio-hora en promedio, haciendo que la energía limpia sea más accesible. También ayuda a resolver un problema llamado "dunkelflaute", períodos cuando hay poco sol y poco viento al mismo tiempo. Al usar ambas fuentes, estos momentos ocurren mucho menos, por lo que las redes eléctricas dependen menos de combustibles fósiles como el carbón y el gas.

**Próximo paso** – Los planificadores de energía pueden usar estos hallazgos para diseñar mejores sistemas que mezclen solar, eólica y almacenamiento. Este enfoque es especialmente útil en regiones del norte donde los días de invierno son cortos y solo la energía solar no es suficiente. Con el tiempo, esto podría llevar a electricidad más limpia y barata en todo el mundo y menos necesidad de construir nuevas plantas de energía fósil.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Combinar energía solar y eólica con almacenamiento en baterías hace que la energía limpia sea más asequible y confiable, reduciendo la necesidad de combustibles fósiles en todo el mundo.

articles.title: Ancient human settlements boosted biomass of today’s Amazon rainforest
articles.summary: Rainforest with a history of human occupation has 2.8 per cent greater biomass, on average, than untouched regions, and this means we might have slightly overestimated Amazonian biomass by mainly assessing formerly occupied areas
articles.content:
Rainforest with a history of human occupation has 2.8 per cent greater biomass, on average, than untouched regions, and this means we might have slightly overestimated Amazonian biomass by mainly assessing formerly occupied areas

The Amazon rainforest near Novo Airão city in Brazil Marcio Isensee e Sá/Getty Images

Ancient human civilisations in the Amazon have had a lasting beneficial impact on the rainforest. Places with a history of human occupation have, on average, 2.8 per cent greater biomass than unoccupied areas. This could affect estimates of how much carbon is stored in these rainforests and help spot previously unknown historical human sites.

Past studies have revealed that human societies in the Amazon, before the arrival of Europeans, altered landscapes by domesticating certain plants and boosted crop productivity by piling up biodegradable waste to create particularly fertile soils known as dark earth, or terra preta.

To get a better idea of how historical human occupation of the Amazon – which is estimated to have involved many millions of people – has altered the forests, Chris Doughty at Northern Arizona University and his colleagues began by working much further north at the archaeological site of Xmakabatun, a Maya city in what is now Guatemala, which was occupied from about 400 BC to AD 800.

Advertisement

The site was chosen because there is a wealth of information about past occupation in the region from mapping it with high-resolution airborne laser imaging.

Doughty and his colleagues analysed the present-day forest along 29 transects through the now-overgrown ancient stone city. Each transect was 30 metres long; nine of them incorporated ancient buildings, 11 went through former agricultural terraces, and nine were in regions of forest that have never been modified.

“It is really incredible, because on the lidar you can see these perfectly preserved ruins, but when you’re actually there, you can’t see a thing,” says Doughty. “We couldn’t have done it without the lidar data directing us to these places.”

Free newsletter Sign up to The Earth Edition Sign up to newsletter

Among other factors, the team estimated the total amount of biomass in each transect by measuring the diameter of tree trunks and their height. They also measured leaf mass and identified how many of the trees were five frequently domesticated species, including the breadnut (Brosimum alicastrum), grown for food and timber, and the copal tree (Protium copal), grown for its resinous incense.

“We saw some significant structural differences,” says Doughty. Crucially, they discovered there was greater biomass where ancient human-built structures sat than on former agricultural terraces, or on undisturbed sites. At both the structures and terraced agricultural areas, there were also more of the frequently domesticated tree species. The trees with fruit often grow slowly, but end up bigger and have more biomass, says Doughty.

“Because we know that there are legacies of past soil modifications, fire and cultivation for modern plant communities, it seems logical that those activities have also altered plant trait compositions,” says Crystal McMichael at the University of Amsterdam, who wasn’t involved in the work.

To see if the same changes could be seen by remote sensing from above, Doughty and his colleagues looked at data on biomass and leaf traits in the region around Xmakabatun, gleaned via lidar studies and Sentinel-2 satellite observations. This revealed a reduction in leaf mass and higher biomass at more densely settled archaeological sites than at control sites with no evidence of past human modification.

With the pattern corroborated, the team moved on to the Amazon, where it is harder to trace past human habitation because communities there had little access to stone for building permanent structures, instead building with earth. They focused similar remote sensing techniques on 500 areas listed in archaeological data sets as featuring fertile dark earth and almost a thousand additional areas with earthworks known as geoglyphs – both implying past habitation. They compared these with 3000 randomly chosen control sites.

Overall, they found that forests at dark-earth sites were shorter but had about 6 per cent more foliage than control sites, and forests near geoglyphs were taller, so had more biomass overall despite the trees being about 20 per cent less bulky in their middle sections than those in control plots. From this, the team has estimated that ancient human occupation has increased modern Amazonian biomass by, on average, 2.8 per cent, equivalent to 0.8 per cent of the globe’s above-ground stores of carbon.

This might mean evaluations of the Amazon rainforest’s biomass – and thus how much carbon is stored there – are slightly overestimated, says Doughty, because current figures are based on surveys in accessible places, which are often where people have formerly lived, so may also be areas with higher-than-normal biomass.

Vinicius Peripato at the Tropical Ecosystems and Environmental Sciences Laboratory at Brazil’s National Institute for Space Research, who wasn’t involved in the research, says the work could help us understand inaccessible rainforest areas. “The ability to detect the effects of ancient human occupation on present-day forest structure using remote-sensing products allows us to investigate these patterns even in remote forest areas.”

The findings have another implication, says Doughty: they suggest it might be possible to spot previously unknown areas where humans have lived in the past. “You could say biomass is better explained where you have archaeology, but you could also potentially use biomass to predict archaeology,” he says.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery that ancient human settlements have positively influenced the biomass of the Amazon rainforest, which has broad implications for understanding carbon storage and historical human impact on ecosystems. This finding advances knowledge in environmental science and conservation, with potential to improve carbon accounting and archaeological detection, benefiting society's understanding of climate and history.
articles.personality_title: Ancient human settlements helped increase biomass in the Amazon rainforest
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have long studied the Amazon rainforest to understand its size and how much carbon it stores. The Amazon is a huge forest that plays an important role in the Earth's climate. People have lived there for thousands of years, but it was unclear how these ancient communities affected the forest.

**What happened** – Researchers studied old Maya sites in Guatemala and places in the Amazon rainforest where ancient people lived. Using special laser and satellite tools, they measured tree sizes and types in areas with ancient buildings or farming terraces and compared them to untouched forests. They found that forests near ancient human sites had about 2.8% more biomass, which means more living plant material.

**Impact** – This discovery shows that ancient people changed the forest in ways that helped it grow more plants and trees. This is important because scientists often estimate the Amazon’s carbon storage by looking at areas where people once lived, which might make the forest seem bigger or store more carbon than it actually does. The study also suggests we can use forest measurements to find hidden ancient settlements.

**What's next step** – Scientists will use these findings to improve how they measure the Amazon’s biomass and carbon storage. They may also search for unknown ancient human sites by looking for areas with unusual forest growth. This could help us better understand both the history of people in the Amazon and how forests store carbon today.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Ancient human settlements have left a lasting mark by increasing plant growth in the Amazon rainforest, helping scientists better measure forest carbon and discover hidden archaeological sites.

articles.title: Photographer Federico Veronesi: 'I've been in love with African wildlife since I was three'
articles.summary: The winner of this year's Wildlife Photographer of the Year award has told FRANCE 24 that his winning picture reveals a lot about the complexity of an elephant's soul and feelings. At first glance the image seems to show a mother elephant playing with her calf, but in fact it is a female carrying another elephant's dead calf. Photographer Federico Veronesi told us how he fell in love in Kenya as a six-year-old child and ended up moving there to fulfil his photography dream. He spoke to us in Perspective.

The winner of this year's Wildlife Photographer of the Year award has told FRANCE 24 that his winning picture reveals a lot about the complexity of an elephant's soul and feelings. At first glance the image seems to show a mother elephant playing with her calf, but in fact it is a female carrying another elephant's dead calf. Photographer Federico Veronesi told us how he fell in love in Kenya as a six-year-old child and ended up moving there to fulfil his photography dream. He spoke to us in Perspective.

articles.personality_title: Photographer captures powerful moment revealing elephant emotions
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Federico Veronesi is a photographer who has loved African wildlife since he was very young. He first visited Kenya as a child and later moved there to follow his dream of photographing animals in the wild.

**What happened** – Veronesi won this year’s Wildlife Photographer of the Year award with a striking image. At first, the photo looks like a mother elephant playing with her baby, but it actually shows a female elephant carrying the dead calf of another elephant.

**Impact** – This picture helps people understand that elephants have deep emotions and complex feelings, similar to humans. It shows the sadness and care elephants can have, which is not often seen. This can make people more interested in protecting these animals and their homes.

**What’s next step** – Veronesi’s work may inspire more photographers and conservationists to share stories about wildlife emotions. It could lead to greater support for efforts to protect elephants and other animals in Africa.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A powerful photograph reveals the emotional depth of elephants, encouraging greater care for wildlife conservation.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un photographe capture un moment fort révélant les émotions des éléphants
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Federico Veronesi est un photographe passionné par la faune africaine depuis son enfance. Il a découvert le Kenya lorsqu’il était enfant et y a déménagé plus tard pour réaliser son rêve de photographier les animaux sauvages.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Veronesi a remporté le prix du Photographe de la faune sauvage de l’année grâce à une image saisissante. Au premier regard, la photo semble montrer une mère éléphant jouant avec son petit, mais en réalité, il s’agit d’une femelle portant le cadavre du petit d’un autre éléphant.

**Impact** – Cette photo aide les gens à comprendre que les éléphants ont des émotions profondes et complexes, proches de celles des humains. Elle montre la tristesse et l’attention que les éléphants peuvent éprouver, ce qui est rarement vu. Cela peut encourager à mieux protéger ces animaux et leur habitat.

**Prochaine étape** – Le travail de Veronesi pourrait inspirer d’autres photographes et défenseurs de la nature à partager les émotions des animaux sauvages. Cela pourrait renforcer le soutien pour la protection des éléphants et d’autres espèces en Afrique.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Une photo puissante révèle la profondeur émotionnelle des éléphants, encourageant une meilleure protection de la faune.
articles.personality_title_es: Un fotógrafo captura un momento poderoso que revela las emociones de los elefantes
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Federico Veronesi es un fotógrafo que ha amado la vida silvestre africana desde niño. Visitó Kenia cuando era pequeño y luego se mudó allí para cumplir su sueño de fotografiar animales en la naturaleza.

**Qué pasó** – Veronesi ganó el premio al Fotógrafo de Vida Silvestre del Año con una imagen impactante. A primera vista, la foto parece mostrar a una elefanta jugando con su cría, pero en realidad es una hembra cargando con el cuerpo sin vida de la cría de otro elefante.

**Impacto** – Esta foto ayuda a las personas a entender que los elefantes tienen emociones profundas y complejas, parecidas a las humanas. Muestra la tristeza y el cuidado que pueden sentir, algo que no se ve a menudo. Esto puede aumentar el interés por proteger a estos animales y sus hogares.

**Próximo paso** – El trabajo de Veronesi podría inspirar a más fotógrafos y conservacionistas a contar historias sobre las emociones de la vida silvestre. Esto podría fortalecer el apoyo para proteger elefantes y otros animales en África.

**Frase clave** – Una fotografía poderosa revela la profundidad emocional de los elefantes, fomentando un mayor cuidado en la conservación de la vida silvestre.
